title: Make the logo bigger
hero: graphite mark block on an ivory layout board
start: A flat ivory layout board about the size of a placemat lies centred on a pale neutral tabletop, its thick card edges crisp and faintly fibrous. Seated on it in a neat grid are six blocks: a long ivory headline bar across the top, two frosted acrylic image tiles with milky edges in the middle, and three narrow ivory text slabs along the bottom. In the upper left corner sits a small matte graphite mark block the size of a sugar cube, its chamfered edges catching light. A slim acid-lime alignment ruler runs along the board's left margin, keeping every block square. A few fine paper fibres and a single scuff mark on the board surface are the only disorder. Everything is balanced, calm and evenly spaced.
end: The same layout board, but the graphite mark block has swollen in visible steps to the size of a brick, with faint seams showing each enlargement like nested shells. It has shoved the headline bar sideways off the top edge, where it hangs mid-fall at an angle. Both frosted image tiles are pushed to the right margin, one tipping over the edge and the other cracked at a corner. The three text slabs are crushed into a creased ivory pile against the lower right corner. The acid-lime alignment ruler has been knocked askew and is sliding off the left edge. Paper dust and small acrylic chips hang in the air, all scattered outward from the graphite block, tracing the push back to its swollen corner.
apocalypse: A wide, low view across an overgrown plain of pale dry grass and ivory paper scraps stretching to a soft horizon. Dominating the midground is the enormous graphite mark block, now the size of a warehouse, weathered and pitted, its chamfered edges chipped and streaked with dust. Around its base, flattened ivory layout slabs lie half sunk in the ground like fallen paving, their surfaces cracked and softened by rain. A frosted acrylic image tile juts from the grass at an angle, its milky face clouded and chipped. In the foreground, a slim graphite gantry crane on four spindly legs is lowering a large square acid-lime grid frame over one of the flattened slabs, measuring it back to its original proportion. Seed heads and fine dust drift through the air.

title: Brief ping-pong
hero: single ivory brief sheet between two in-trays
start: Two matte graphite in-trays, each about the size of a paperback, sit a hand's width apart on a pale neutral tabletop, facing each other with their open fronts aligned. Their brushed sides show fine machining lines and small countersunk screws at the corners. Resting flat in the gap between them is a single ivory brief sheet, crisp and folded once, its blank face slightly lifted at one corner. Clipped to its top edge is one small acid-lime binder clip, the only note so far. To the back left, a frosted acrylic pen cup holds nothing. A little paper dust sits along the tray rims. The layout is symmetrical and still, with the brief waiting to be placed.
end: The same two graphite trays, but the brief sheet is frozen mid-flight in a tall arc between them, sagging under a thick bundle of ivory notes clipped along every edge. Dozens of small graphite binder clips grip layered slips of creased card, and the original acid-lime clip is buried in the middle of the bundle. The overloaded sheet is bending at its fold and shedding slips as it swings; several notes flutter loose below, some already scattered across the tabletop between the trays. The left tray has been knocked backward by the last landing and is tilting on one edge. Faint scuff trails on the table surface run back and forth between the trays, recording every pass.
apocalypse: A deep miniature canyon cut through layered ivory paper strata, viewed from its rim with the far wall fading into haze. On each side of the gorge stands a colossal ruined graphite in-tray, now the size of a cliff dwelling, its brushed walls dented, cracked and streaked with dust. The canyon floor is filled with a sediment of clipped notes, thousands of creased slips and rusted graphite clips compacted into banded layers. The brief sheet itself, grown into a vast weathered sail of ivory card, hangs torn and snagged halfway down the left wall. On the right rim, a slim graphite winch rig on tracked feet has fired an acid-lime anchor cable across the gorge and is drawing the brief firmly into the right-hand tray.

title: Proofing rounds
hero: small graphite stamp press with a tick-mark round dial
start: A small matte graphite stamp press, about the height of a stapler, stands at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. It has a squared frame, a brushed lever arm with a knurled grip and a flat ivory platen. Under the platen lies one crisp ivory proof sheet with faint blank blocks where a layout will sit. On the side of the press is a plain round dial with tick marks and a single slim needle, resting at the first tick. To the right, an empty frosted glass out-tray waits. The acid-lime element is the press's rubber stamp face, clean and untouched, visible beneath the platen. A few paper fibres lie at the base. The scene is neat and ready for one approval.
end: The same graphite stamp press is mid-stroke, lever halfway down, with a fresh ivory proof sliding out from under the platen on the left. The needle on the tick-mark dial has swung almost all the way around. Beside the press rises a tall, leaning column of near-identical proofs, each slightly offset from the last, overflowing the frosted glass out-tray and curving toward the table edge. The top sheets are sliding off in a frozen fan, and several have landed creased on the tabletop. The acid-lime stamp face is still clean, never used. Fine paper dust puffs out from the platen, and a trail of stray proofs runs straight back from the leaning column to the press.
apocalypse: Towering sediment cliffs of compressed ivory proof sheets rise across the landscape, their banded layers slightly offset like rock strata, eroded into ledges and overhangs that recede toward a dusty horizon. Half buried at the foot of the nearest cliff lies the enormous graphite stamp press, tilted on its side, lever arm snapped off and the platen jammed open, streaked with fine grit. Its tick-mark dial has fallen out and lies face up in the scree, its needle bent. Loose proofs have weathered into brittle flakes that drift along the cliff base. On the highest ledge, a slim graphite tracked crawler with a long articulated arm lowers a single acid-lime stamp head onto the top sheet of the cliff, pressing a final approval.

title: Stock photo licensing
hero: three photo prints on a graphite rail with lime tags
start: A slim matte graphite rail about the length of a forearm stands on two short posts across a pale neutral tabletop. Hanging from it on small graphite clips are three ivory photo prints, each the size of a postcard with a crisp white border and a soft, blank image area. From each clip a fine ivory thread leads down to a small acid-lime licence tag, a blank rounded rectangle of card, one tag per print. The tags hang straight and still. To the left, an empty frosted acrylic box waits for more prints. The rail's brushed surface shows faint machining lines, and a thin film of dust sits along the tabletop near the posts.
end: The same graphite rail is now crowded with prints jammed edge to edge, and the rail bows in the middle under their weight. The ivory threads have twisted into loose knots between neighbouring clips, and several acid-lime licence tags have slipped free and are frozen mid-fall toward the table. Untagged prints slide off the rail at the right end and fan across the tabletop, overlapping and curling at the corners. The frosted acrylic box has been knocked over, spilling more prints. A single lime tag lies face down under a print where no one will find it. Paper dust and a few loose fibres float in the air, and the spill spreads outward from the bowed middle of the rail.
apocalypse: A white salt flat stretches flat and cracked to a sharp, distant horizon, its polygonal crust scattered with thousands of weathered ivory photo prints, curled, sun-bleached and half fused into the ground. In the midground, the graphite rail has become a long ruined colonnade, its posts leaning and one section collapsed into the crust. Snapped clips the size of doorways dangle from it, and knotted ivory threads trail across the flat like dried riverbeds. Toward the right, a slim graphite rail cart runs on a newly laid track beside the colonnade, its long needle arm threading a single acid-lime tag back onto one recovered print and clipping it upright. Fine salt dust hangs low over the ground.

title: Colour mismatch
hero: frosted acrylic swatch tile beside an ivory printed swatch
start: On a pale neutral tabletop, a frosted acrylic tile about the size of a playing card stands upright in a matte graphite stand, lit softly from within so its milky surface glows a clean acid-lime. This backlit tile is the scene's single lime element and the target colour. Directly in front of it lies a printed ivory card swatch of the same size, its patch a slightly duller, greener tone that almost matches. A small graphite loupe sits beside the card, and a sandblasted glass ruler lies parallel to the edge. The card's fibres and faint ink grain are visible up close. Everything is aligned and orderly, the only flaw being the small gap in tone between tile and print.
end: The same graphite stand and glowing acid-lime acrylic tile remain at the back, but in front of them a long fan of printed swatch cards now spreads across the tabletop toward the viewer. Each card was copied from the previous one, and the tones drift in visible steps from a soft yellow-green to olive, then grey, then a flat muddy beige at the far end. The newest cards are still sliding off the fan and one is frozen mid-flip at the table edge. The loupe has been knocked over and rolled into the stack, and the glass ruler lies crooked beneath several cards. Fine ink dust and paper fibres hang above the fan, which traces straight back to the first card beside the tile.
apocalypse: A shallow flooded basin stretches toward a misty horizon, its still grey water scattered with low islands made of stacked swatch cards, swollen, faded and warped into terraced mounds. The tones of the islands drift from pale green near the centre to dull beige at the edges. In the midground, the enormous graphite stand rises from the water like a ruined tower, and the frosted acrylic tile it once held lies cracked and clouded, half submerged at its base. Tide lines of ink stain the card islands. On the nearest island, a slim graphite tripod calibration rig on long thin legs holds an acid-lime reference lens over the first swatch, a fine lime probe pressing its patch back toward the right tone.

title: File too big to send
hero: oversized graphite file crate at a narrow mail slot
start: A narrow ivory card mail slot, about the width of a hand, is set into a low graphite wall at the back of a pale neutral tabletop, with a short frosted acrylic chute leading away behind it. In the foreground sits an oversized matte graphite file crate the size of a shoebox, packed with ivory folders whose blank tabs stick up unevenly. The crate's corners are chamfered and its sides carry bolted handles. It is clearly wider than the slot. A small acid-lime push plate is fixed to the back of the crate, ready to send it forward. Fine dust gathers along the base of the wall. The scene is orderly, with the single problem of size mismatch plain to see.
end: The same graphite crate has been driven into the ivory mail slot and is wedged there at an angle, its front corners crumpled and one side panel split open along a seam. Ivory folders burst out in chunks, some forced through the slot and tumbling down the frosted acrylic chute in uneven clumps, others spilling backwards onto the tabletop. The slot's card frame is torn and bulging, and the graphite wall has cracked around it. The acid-lime push plate is still pressed against the crate's back, bent from the strain. Loose sheets and dust hang in the air on both sides of the wall, and the scatter traces back to the split crate.
apocalypse: A rocky mountain pass of pale grey scree climbs toward a hazy ridge, with a collapsed tunnel mouth cut into the cliff at its head. The tunnel's arch is formed from the ruined ivory mail slot, now enormous, its card edges swollen and crumbling, the graphite wall around it cracked into slabs. Piled against the blocked entrance are huge broken fragments of the graphite file crate, its handles snapped and side panels bent, with weathered ivory folders compacted into drifts between them. A trickle of loose sheets escapes through a narrow gap at the top. In the foreground, a slim graphite boring conveyor on crawler tracks has an acid-lime cutting head biting into the tunnel's edge, widening the passage.

title: Expired transfer link
hero: frosted acrylic pneumatic tube with a file cartridge
start: A clear run of sandblasted frosted glass pneumatic tube, about the thickness of a wrist, arcs across a pale neutral tabletop from a graphite sender port on the left to a graphite receiver on the right, supported by slim brushed brackets. Inside the tube, just past the start, sits a single matte graphite file cartridge with ribbed end caps. On top of the sender port is a small plain dial with tick marks, its acid-lime needle sweeping down toward the last tick. That needle is the only lime element. Faint dust dulls the glass, and fine machining lines show on the brackets. Everything is aligned and in transit, with time quietly running out.
end: The same frosted glass tube, but the acid-lime needle on the sender dial has hit its last tick and the tube has lost pressure. The line has sagged, and one bracket has snapped so the tube hangs open at a joint in the middle. The graphite file cartridge has slid backward and dropped through the gap, frozen mid-fall toward the tabletop, while several more cartridges queued behind it tumble out of the sender port. Two already lie on the table, one rolling toward the edge with a loosened end cap. A puff of frosted dust hangs where the tube separated, and the fallen cartridges lie in a line directly beneath the broken joint.
apocalypse: A quiet fog valley fills the frame, with low mist lying between pale ridges and a soft horizon barely visible. Striding across the valley is the ruined pneumatic tube, now an aqueduct of cracked, frosted glass sections the size of train carriages, carried on tall graphite brackets. One span in the middle has fallen, its broken ends hanging open over the valley floor. Below the gap, a field of weathered graphite cartridges lies scattered and half sunk in the damp ground, their end caps rusted and missing. The enormous sender dial lies face down in the grass. A slim graphite crane with a long boom stands in the fog, lowering a new acid-lime tube section to reconnect the two broken ends.

title: Ad size explosion
hero: ivory ad frame on a graphite easel
start: A small matte graphite easel, about the height of a wine bottle, stands in the centre of a pale neutral tabletop with slim legs and a knurled height knob. On it rests one finished ad frame: a crisp ivory card panel inside a thin brushed graphite border, with blank blocks for image and headline. A single acid-lime button shape sits in the lower right corner of the ad, the one element that has just been changed. Beside the easel lie a graphite craft knife and a frosted acrylic cutting ruler, both perfectly aligned. Light dust rests on the table. The scene is calm, with one small edit waiting to be applied.
end: The same graphite easel is now surrounded by dozens of ad frames in every proportion, tall skinny banners, wide strips, tiny squares and oversized panels, fanning outward across the tabletop and stacked against each other. Each is a copy of the original, and each has its acid-lime button placed slightly differently, some cut in half by the border, some floating. The easel is leaning under the weight of frames propped against it. A tall banner is toppling over at the back, and a small square is frozen mid-slide off the table's edge. Card offcuts and graphite border shavings are scattered around the craft knife, and the fan radiates outward from the easel.
apocalypse: A terraced quarry cut into pale ivory card stone descends in wide steps toward a hazy basin, seen from a high edge. Each terrace is crowded with enormous ad frames in mismatched proportions, leaning in rows, cracked, bleached and chipped at their graphite borders. At the bottom of the quarry the original easel stands as a toppled ruin, legs snapped and splayed like a fallen tower. Offcuts form drifts along the terrace walls. On the upper terrace, a slim graphite gantry on straight rails holds an acid-lime cutting frame over a single oversized panel, trimming it down to a clean proportion. A neat row of three already-resized frames stands beside the gantry.

title: Tracking tag chaos
hero: frosted acrylic tracking pipe fed by link tokens
start: A single frosted acrylic pipe, about the width of a thumb, runs straight across a pale neutral tabletop from an ivory card intake funnel on the left to a graphite collection tray on the right. Its milky walls glow faintly from inside. Lined up at the funnel are six small matte graphite link tokens, like coin-sized discs with chamfered edges, each carrying an identical folded ivory tag. The acid-lime element is a narrow band painted around the funnel mouth, marking the one agreed entry point. Tokens already inside the pipe can be seen as soft shadows sliding through. Dust and fine scuffs mark the tabletop near the funnel.
end: The same frosted acrylic pipe has sprouted branches: extra tubes are jammed into it at odd angles, splitting the line into four channels leading to different trays and one leading off the table edge. Graphite tokens tagged in mismatched ways, with tags folded, torn, doubled or missing, are pouring in at the funnel, and the acid-lime band is now hidden under a pile-up of tokens. Several tokens are frozen mid-drop from a branch that ends in open air. The original collection tray holds only one token, while the other trays overflow. Loose ivory tags flutter above the branches, and the sprawl traces back to the crowded funnel.
apocalypse: A silted river delta spreads to a low horizon, seen from above at a slight angle, its many channels choked with weathered graphite tokens and ivory sediment. The channels are the collapsed branches of the old pipe, now enormous frosted acrylic culverts cracked open and overgrown with pale reeds. Shallow pools gleam between banks of compacted tags, and a few tokens lie stranded on sandbars. In the midground, the ruined intake funnel stands half buried like a broken amphitheatre. At the fork nearest the camera, a slim graphite sluice rig on stilts is lowering a single acid-lime gate across the side channels, diverting the flow of tokens back into one clear main channel.

title: Midnight scheduled post
hero: graphite publishing slot with a timer dial
start: A compact matte graphite publishing unit, about the size of a toaster, sits on a pale neutral tabletop with a narrow slot on its front face. Feeding into its back is a short ivory card conveyor holding four post cards standing upright in a tidy queue, blank faces forward. On top of the unit is a plain round dial with tick marks and a slim graphite hand, with a single acid-lime tick marking the planned send time. Beside the unit, a cold frosted glass mug and a folded ivory note suggest someone has left for the evening. The room's light is soft and ordinary. Everything waits in order.
end: The same graphite publishing unit, now in a dim room lit only by the faint glow from its slot. The dial's hand has slipped far past the acid-lime tick and is spinning, blurred. Post cards are firing out of the slot one after another, frozen mid-air in a long arc across the dark tabletop, some tumbling end over end, several already scattered and face down beyond the table edge. The ivory conveyor behind is empty and still running, its belt creased. The frosted glass mug has been knocked over by a stray card. Fine paper dust hangs in the glow, and every card's path traces straight back to the slot.
apocalypse: A dark, low-lit moorland of grey heather and scattered ivory cards stretches to a faint horizon under a dim sky. In the midground, the enormous graphite publishing unit lies toppled on its side like a fallen monument, its slot cracked open and its surface pitted and streaked with damp. The timer dial has broken away and lies half sunk in the peat, its hand bent over the face. Thousands of weathered post cards are strewn in a long fan across the moor, curled and softened by rain. A slim graphite crane rig on three tall legs stands over the dial, its fine arm setting a new acid-lime hand back in place, the first steady mark in the dark landscape.

title: Everything is urgent
hero: row of ivory task cards, one flagged
start: A neat row of five ivory task cards, each the size of a coaster with crisp edges and blank faces, stands upright in slim graphite card holders along a pale neutral tabletop. Only the middle card carries a small flag: a thin graphite pin with a triangular acid-lime pennant, clearly marking the one task that matters today. The other cards are plain and evenly spaced. At the back, a frosted acrylic pin box holds a few spare graphite pins. The card fibres show fine grain and a faint crease on one corner. The scene is quiet, with a single clear priority.
end: The same row of task cards is now buried under flags. Graphite pins with ivory pennants are stuck into every card, then into the pennants themselves, forming bristling thickets that bend the cards backward in their holders. The original acid-lime pennant is barely visible deep inside the middle thicket. The frosted pin box has been emptied and knocked on its side. Two cards have collapsed under the weight and are frozen mid-fall, shedding pins across the tabletop. Loose pennants float down through the air. Nothing of the actual task faces can be seen anymore, and the heaviest pile sits exactly where the first flag was.
apocalypse: A windswept tundra of pale gravel and ivory card fragments stretches to a flat horizon, bristling with countless weathered flags. Enormous graphite pins stand at every angle like dead trees, their faded ivory pennants torn, bleached and flapping in the wind. Toppled task cards the size of barns lie half buried among them, their faces lost under the flag thickets. In the midground, a long slim graphite sorting rack on crawler legs moves slowly across the ground, plucking pins from the gravel with fine arms. It has raised only three flags onto its top rail, and one of them bears an acid-lime pennant standing clearly above the rest.

title: Got a sec?
hero: frosted acrylic focus block on a graphite platform
start: A small matte graphite platform, about the size of a saucer, stands on a short column in the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. On it sits a single frosted acrylic focus block, a cube with milky edges and a soft internal glow, placed dead centre. Around the platform, three slim graphite tapping arms on hinged mounts rest folded down at the edges of the table, still. A cold ivory paper cup sits nearby. The acid-lime element is a thin ring painted around the platform's rim, marking the spot where the block belongs. Faint dust and fine scuffs mark the platform's surface. Everything is balanced and quiet.
end: The same graphite platform, but the three tapping arms have swung up and are frozen at the end of a nudge, their tips extended toward the platform. The focus block has been knocked off and is caught mid-tumble in the air, its glow flickering. On the tabletop beyond, a trail of scuff marks and small acrylic chips shows the landing spots from earlier nudges, each one further from the platform than the last. The acid-lime ring on the platform rim is empty. The ivory cup has tipped, spilling a small puddle. Dust hangs where the arms swung, and the landing trail leads straight back to the empty ring.
apocalypse: A flooded ruin of a wide tidal marsh spreads to a low horizon, shallow still water reflecting a pale sky. In the midground, the enormous graphite platform stands on its cracked column like a sinking tower, water lapping its base. The focus block, now the size of a house, has cracked into several frosted slabs that lie in a line across the shallows, each further from the platform than the last. The tapping arms tower beside it, rusted and frozen at odd angles. On the platform top, a slim graphite rig has raised a curved acid-lime shield around the platform rim and is lifting the largest recovered slab back into place behind it.

title: Context switching
hero: small graphite rotating desk ringed by six task trays
start: A small round matte graphite desk, about the size of a dinner plate, sits on a turntable base at the centre of a pale neutral tabletop. Arranged around it in a neat circle are six shallow ivory card task trays, each holding a single blank work sheet. A slim graphite writing arm on the desk points at one tray. The acid-lime element is a small indicator notch on the desk's rim showing the current facing direction. The trays are evenly spaced like hours on a dial. Fine paper fibres and a faint circular scuff on the tabletop show where the desk turns. Everything is still and ordered.
end: The same graphite desk is spinning fast on its turntable, motion-blurred at its edges, with the acid-lime notch smeared into a faint streak. Every one of the six ivory trays now holds a half-finished sheet: one partly folded, one half torn, one with a graphite pencil line stopping mid-stroke. The writing arm has flung loose sheets outward, frozen in a spiral of airborne paper around the desk. Two trays have been knocked askew and one has tipped over, spilling its work. Dust and paper shreds hang in a ring above the table. The spiral of debris leads back to the spinning desk.
apocalypse: A windswept hilltop of pale scrub and ivory paper drifts overlooks a hazy valley. Crowning the hill is the enormous graphite desk, seized on its cracked turntable, tilted at an angle and streaked with dust. Around it in a wide, broken ring lie six ruined ivory trays the size of courtyards, each filled with weathered half-finished sheets now bleached and matted into the ground. A spiral of old paper debris still curls outward across the hillside. Beside the desk's base, a slim graphite brake rig has clamped an acid-lime caliper onto the turntable edge, holding the desk still and facing one single tray.

title: Blocked by another team
hero: graphite gate where two conveyor lines meet
start: Two slim ivory card conveyor belts, each about the width of a ruler, run across a pale neutral tabletop and meet at a single matte graphite gate, a squared frame with a sliding shutter. Beyond the gate, one shared belt continues toward the back. On the waiting line sit three small graphite work blocks spaced evenly, and the other line carries two more. The shutter is closed. The acid-lime element is a small handle on the gate's top edge, the lever that would open it. Belt surfaces show fine fibre and slight wear, and the gate's fasteners are neatly countersunk. The scene is orderly, with a short wait at the gate.
end: The same graphite gate stands shut, but the waiting belt is packed solid with work blocks jammed nose to tail. Blocks have climbed on top of each other in a wedge against the shutter and are spilling over the belt's rails, several frozen mid-fall toward the tabletop. The belt surface is buckled and torn at the pile-up. The second line is backing up too, its blocks pushed sideways. The acid-lime handle on top of the gate is untouched. The belt beyond the gate is empty and clean. Dust and fibre shreds hang over the pile, and the jam spreads backward from the closed shutter along both lines.
apocalypse: A wide glacier descends between pale mountain walls toward a misty horizon, its surface crevassed and streaked with ivory grit. Locked in the ice are the two enormous conveyor belts, frozen into long ridges, with thousands of graphite work blocks trapped in compacted rows behind a colossal graphite gate that stands half buried at the glacier's foot, its shutter rusted shut. Ice has built up against the gate like a frozen wave. On a ledge beside it, a slim graphite chain drive rig with an acid-lime sprocket has been bolted to the gate frame and is beginning to haul the shutter up, a narrow crack of light showing beneath.

title: Duplicate work
hero: twin graphite workbenches building the same part
start: Two identical small matte graphite workbenches, each about the size of a shoebox, stand side by side on a pale neutral tabletop, separated by a thin frosted acrylic partition. Each bench has a tiny vice and holds the same half-built part: a ribbed ivory card bracket. Beside each bench sits a neat ivory tray holding a single finished bracket. The partition keeps either bench from seeing the other. The acid-lime element is a small spec card propped at the front of the left bench only, the one shared plan. Fine machining lines, paper fibres and a light dust film cover both benches. Everything is mirrored and orderly.
end: The same twin benches are now overflowing with identical ivory brackets. Each tray has disappeared under a heap of parts, and duplicates are stacked in towers along both benches, identical in every fold. Brackets spill down both sides of the frosted partition, and the two heaps are meeting at its base in a jumbled pile. One tower is frozen mid-collapse, parts sliding across the tabletop. The acid-lime spec card has been pushed over and lies half buried on the left bench. Card dust hangs above both heaps, and the two spills mirror each other exactly back to their benches.
apocalypse: Twin badland mesas of layered ivory sediment rise side by side from a dusty plain, separated by a narrow gully, with a hazy horizon behind them. Each mesa is capped by the ruined, weathered hulk of an enormous graphite workbench, identical, cracked and leaning in the same direction. Their slopes are formed from compacted drifts of identical brackets, eroded into matching ridges. The frosted partition stands in the gully as a cracked glass wall. On the plain in front, a slim graphite rail rig is laying an acid-lime merge track that begins at the foot of each mesa and joins the two lines into one, with a single bracket riding along it.

title: Single point of knowledge
hero: small graphite vault with one key module
start: A small matte graphite vault, about the size of a bread box, stands on a pale neutral tabletop with a thick circular door, a ring of bolts and chamfered hinges. Slotted into the centre of the door is a single key module, a slim graphite cartridge with an acid-lime grip, the only thing that opens the vault. In front of the vault, one ivory folder rests on a small tray, waiting to be filed. A cold frosted glass mug sits to the side. Machining lines on the door and faint dust on the bolt heads catch the light. Everything is orderly and depends on that one module.
end: The same graphite vault, but the key module is gone, leaving an empty slot in the door; the acid-lime grip lies alone on a nearby desk chair seat beside a folded jacket, its owner away. In front of the vault, a long queue of ivory folders, trays and graphite boxes has formed, stacked and pressed against the door, the front ones buckling. The line bends across the tabletop and new folders are frozen mid-slide as they join the back. A tray has tipped, spilling sheets. Dust hangs in the air above the queue, and the whole jam points back to the empty slot.
apocalypse: A narrow rocky gorge of pale stone narrows toward a hazy distant bend. Built into the gorge wall is the enormous graphite vault door, now a sealed ruin, its bolts corroded, its surface streaked with mineral stains, the empty key slot a dark recess high above the ground. Stretching away down the gorge floor is a long queue of weathered ivory folders and graphite boxes, the size of shipping containers, compacted and half buried in scree. In front of the door, a slim graphite fabrication rig on four jointed legs is machining a new acid-lime key module, fine metal shavings curling from the cutter.

title: Vague ticket
hero: blank ivory ticket card in a graphite intake tray
start: A shallow matte graphite intake tray, about the size of a postcard, sits on a pale neutral tabletop, its brushed rim chamfered and fixed with four small countersunk screws. In it lies a single ivory ticket card, thick and crisp, completely blank, with a round punched hole at one end and a faint diagonal crease across the middle. The acid-lime element is a small spring clip on the tray's front lip, holding the ticket in place for whoever picks it up. To the right, a graphite pen rests untouched on a frosted acrylic block with milky edges. Behind the tray stands an empty ivory out-tray. A little dust gathers in the tray corners. Everything is neat and calm; the only problem is how little the ticket says.
end: The same graphite tray and blank ticket, but the card is now ringed by dozens of looped ivory paper strips orbiting around it at different heights, each loop a question folded back on itself. The loops are layered in tilted rings like the paths of small satellites, frozen mid-circle, some snagged on each other and tearing. New loops are budding off the outer rings and flying outward, one frozen mid-spin over the table edge. The acid-lime clip still holds the ticket, which remains blank. The graphite pen has been knocked from its acrylic block and is rolling away, and the ivory out-tray is still empty. Paper shreds and dust hang within the rings, and every orbit is centred on the blank card.
apocalypse: A wide impact crater of pale ivory dust fills the frame, its soft raised rim curving away toward a hazy horizon. Above the crater's centre, on a tall bent graphite mast, hangs a seized orbiting frame: a ring of rusted graphite rails still holding a few loops of paper, now brittle, grey and split. On the crater floor lies the enormous blank ticket card, the size of a sports field, cracked along its old crease and weathered at the punched hole, with drifts of fallen loops banked up against its edges like snow. The old intake tray lies buckled beneath it. On the crater's rim, a slim graphite boom rig on splayed legs reaches down and presses an acid-lime stamp onto the card, leaving a clean diagram of plain boxes and connecting lines.

title: Purchase order relay
hero: ivory purchase-order form on a graphite tray
start: A single ivory purchase-order form, crisp and folded once, lies on a small matte graphite tray at the front of a pale neutral tabletop. Along its lower edge sit three empty signature boxes drawn as plain rectangles, with no writing anywhere. Behind it, three more graphite trays stand in a short neat row on slim posts, stepping back toward the rear like stations on a route, each with brushed sides and small hex bolts. The acid-lime element is a narrow ribbon bookmark tucked under the form on the first tray, marking where it must return once signed. A cold frosted glass mug stands beside the last tray. Fine paper fibres and a trace of dust mark the table. The relay route is short and clear.
end: The same first tray, but the relay has sprawled. Dozens of extra graphite trays now stand across the tabletop on posts of different heights, stacked, angled and branching off in every direction like a spreading rail network. Copies of the form sit on many of them, each carrying more rows of empty signature boxes than the last. One sheet is frozen mid-pass between two distant trays, curling in the air, and several are sliding off the far trays and over the table edge. A tray near the back has tipped, dropping a fan of forms. The acid-lime ribbon still lies on the original first tray, which stays empty. Dust hangs over the network, and every branch radiates out from that first tray.
apocalypse: A long dry riverbed of cracked pale mud winds across a flat steppe toward a far, hazy horizon. Along both banks stand ruined graphite trays the size of small stations, on toppled or leaning posts, rusted and pitted, forming a broken relay route that meanders out of sight. The riverbed is littered with weathered ivory forms, softened and curled, banked in shallow drifts against stones and snagged in dry grass. In the foreground, the original first tray sits cracked and half buried, its surface dusty. A slim graphite shuttle rig running on a single thin monorail is carrying one recovered form in an acid-lime clasp, heading straight back down the route toward that first tray, its rail laid neatly over the mud.

title: Signature chase
hero: ivory document on a small graphite rail cart
start: A slim matte graphite rail track, about the length of a forearm, curves gently across a pale neutral tabletop on small ivory card sleepers. On it sits a small rail cart the size of a matchbox with brushed side panels and tiny spoked wheels, carrying a single ivory document folded once. Along the route stand three small graphite signing posts, each with a hinged barrier arm raised and a blank ivory flap. The acid-lime element is the cart's front bumper plate, leading the way. Beside the track, a cold frosted glass mug on an empty desk corner shows the signer has stepped out. Rails show fine machining lines, and faint dust rests on the sleepers. Everything is ordered and ready to move.
end: The same graphite track, but the cart has stalled at the first signing post, its acid-lime bumper pressed against a lowered barrier arm. Behind it, a queue of identical carts carrying ivory documents stretches back around the curve, packed nose to tail. The rearmost carts have been shunted off the rails and are frozen mid-tip, documents sliding out of them onto the tabletop in a loose fan. The blank flap on the first post hangs open, unsigned. The other two posts further along the line stand with their barriers down too, and the track beyond is empty. Dust and paper fibres hang over the pile-up, and the derailments trace back along the queue to the one stopped cart.
apocalypse: A steep mountainside of loose pale scree drops toward a hazy valley, with a switchback railway cut into it in long zigzags. The enormous graphite rails are snapped and twisted at several bends. A long line of derailed carts, each now the size of a freight wagon, lies tumbled down the slope, rusted, dented and half buried, their ivory documents weathered into flaking sheets scattered across the rocks. The old signing posts stand at every switchback like tall rusted signal towers, barrier arms still lowered. In the foreground, a slim graphite track-laying rig on crawler feet is extending a new acid-lime bypass rail in a clean curve around the stalled posts, and one recovered cart is already rolling along it.

title: Net-90 invoice
hero: ivory invoice envelope in a graphite waiting tray
start: A small matte graphite waiting tray, about the size of a paperback, sits on a pale neutral tabletop with chamfered corners and a brushed finish. In it lies a single ivory invoice envelope, crisp at the folds, with a blank address panel and a deckled flap. The acid-lime element is a small round seal on the envelope's flap, marking it as due. To the right stands a frosted acrylic desk calendar block showing a plain dial with tick marks, its hand only a little way round. Behind the tray, an empty ivory out-tray waits for payment to come back. A faint dust ring marks the tray's base. The scene is still, and the invoice is simply waiting.
end: The same graphite tray is sinking under a tall mound of ivory reminder envelopes piled on top of the original invoice, each one slightly larger and heavier than the last, flaps crumpled and edges bent. The tray has tilted, one corner pressed down and denting the tabletop, and envelopes are sliding off the high side, frozen mid-fall in a spray. The acid-lime seal of the first envelope shows only as a sliver at the bottom of the pile. The calendar block has been knocked over and lies face down, and the out-tray behind is still empty. Paper dust drifts above the heap, and the whole mound slopes down toward the sinking corner.
apocalypse: A frozen lake of pale grey ice stretches toward a snowy, hazy horizon, buried in drifts of weathered ivory envelopes compacted into long ridges by the wind. The ice is cracked in branching lines. In the midground, the enormous graphite waiting tray is half sunk into the ice and tilted at a steep angle, rimed with frost, with the mound of reminders frozen solid on top of it like a small glacier. A cold ruined out-tray stands far across the ice, empty. In the foreground, a slim graphite conveyor on long ski runners has hooked the original invoice from the base of the frozen mound with an acid-lime grabber and is carrying it across the ice toward the out-tray.

title: Thermostat war
hero: graphite thermostat dial on a miniature office wall
start: A low ivory card wall about the height of a tissue box stands across the back of a pale neutral tabletop, its top edge crisp and slightly fibrous. Mounted at its centre is a round matte graphite thermostat dial with a knurled bezel and a plain face of tick marks. The acid-lime element is the dial's pointer, set straight up to the middle. In front of the wall, four small graphite desks sit in an even row, each with a folded ivory note and a frosted glass cup. A small ivory jacket hangs over one desk chair, and a folded cardigan lies on another. Fine machining lines on the bezel and light dust along the wall top show the scale. Everything is balanced and comfortable.
end: The same graphite dial is being turned hard, its acid-lime pointer frozen mid-swing with a blurred arc showing it has been yanked back and forth. The desks below are split. The two on the left are coated in white frost, their frosted glass cups cracked and the ivory jacket stiff over its chair. The two on the right shimmer in heat haze, their ivory notes curling and browned at the edges, and the cardigan has been flung onto the floor. A thin line of meltwater runs along the table between the zones. Frost crystals hang in the cold air and warm dust rises on the right, and both extremes trace straight back to the dial.
apocalypse: A wide cracked plain stretches to a hazy horizon, split sharply down the middle. The left half lies under white frost and ice ridges, the right half is scorched and broken into dry, pale, curling plates. Along the dividing line runs the enormous ivory wall, now a crumbling ruin with gaps and fallen sections, and the graphite thermostat dial hangs off it at a tilt, its bezel cracked and face pitted. Toppled desks lie half frozen in ice on one side and half baked into the dry crust on the other. At the dividing line, a slim graphite regulator mast rig on three legs extends an acid-lime balancing arm over both zones, and a narrow band of even, neutral ground is spreading out from its base.

title: Kitchen mug tower
hero: one unwashed ivory mug in a small office-kitchen sink
start: A small ivory office-kitchen sink, about the size of a lunchbox, is set into a pale neutral counter, its basin smooth with a brushed graphite tap and a round graphite drain. In the basin rests one unwashed matte ivory mug with a faint brown coffee ring inside and a tiny chip on its rim. The acid-lime element is this mug's handle, the one clue to whose mug it is. Beside the sink stands an empty frosted acrylic drying rack with a folded ivory cloth hung over its edge, and a sponge sits dry on the drain board. Fine water spots and light dust mark the counter. Everything is tidy apart from the one mug left behind.
end: The same sink is now crowned by a tall leaning tower of mugs stacked rim on rim on the first one, rising well above the graphite tap and curving out over the counter. Ivory, graphite and frosted glass mugs are wedged together at uneven angles, the lower ones cracked under the weight. The top of the tower is frozen mid-topple: one mug is falling toward the floor, another is bouncing off the counter and a third has just shattered beside the rack. The acid-lime handle of the first mug is just visible at the base. Drops of stale coffee spray outward from the falling mugs, and the lean traces straight back to the sink.
apocalypse: A pale shoreline made of broken ceramic shards runs along a quiet grey sea toward a misty horizon. In the midground, the enormous toppled mug tower lies across the beach like a fallen stone column, its mugs cracked, stained and chipped, the outer end sliding into the shallows. Behind it, the ruined sink juts from the shards at an angle, its graphite tap bent and streaked with mineral deposits. Small waves wash shards along the tide line, and old coffee stains mark the rims. In the foreground, a slim graphite sorting rig on tall jointed legs picks through the shard beach with long tweezer arms, setting only the few intact mugs in a neat row on an acid-lime drying rack.

title: Hot-desk shuffle
hero: graphite desk with a lime booking tag
start: A single matte graphite desk, about the size of a hardback book, stands on a pale neutral floor tile, its legs set into slim grooved floor rails that run off in several directions. On the desk sits a small, tidy set of belongings: a frosted glass mug, an ivory notebook with crisp edges and a small graphite desk lamp with a chamfered shade. A cardigan hangs over the back of the matching chair. Hanging from the desk's front edge on a short thread is an acid-lime booking tag, a blank card with a punched hole, showing the desk is claimed for today. Two other desks stand empty nearby. Dust rests in the rail grooves. Everything is organised and in its place.
end: The same graphite desk and its neighbours are now gliding along the floor rails, frozen mid-slide into new positions, with scuff lines on the tile tracing each path. The belongings have been left behind where the desk used to stand: the frosted mug is tipped over in the aisle, the ivory notebook lies splayed open, the lamp has rolled into a rail groove and the cardigan has slipped off onto the floor. The acid-lime tag is still tied to the desk but has swung around and twisted on its thread as the desk moves away. Paper scraps and dust float above the aisles, and the scattered belongings mark the desk's starting spot.
apocalypse: A dry lakebed of cracked pale mud plates stretches to a flat horizon under a dusty haze. Across it, enormous graphite desks lie scattered at random angles, some tipped on their sides, some half sunk in the mud, their surfaces pitted and streaked. Broken floor rails run in interrupted lines through the cracks like old roads. Weathered belongings lie between them: a cracked frosted mug as big as a water tower, a notebook eroded into layered flakes, a lamp shade half buried. In the foreground, a slim graphite gridding rig on thin wheels is rolling out a taut acid-lime floor grid across the mud, and one desk has already been winched upright and set squarely inside its square.

title: Dead whiteboard marker
hero: ivory whiteboard with one streaky stroke above a marker tray
start: A small ivory whiteboard panel, about the size of a placemat, stands upright on a slim graphite easel at the back of a pale neutral tabletop, its surface smooth with faint ghost smudges from old sessions. Across it runs a single faint, streaky grey stroke, broken into dry gaps where the marker ran out. Below the board, a narrow graphite tray holds three capped graphite markers lined up neatly. The acid-lime element is the loose cap of the marker that made the stroke, lying on the tray's edge beside it. A folded ivory cloth rests on the table to the left. Fine dust sits along the tray lip. Everything is orderly, but the stroke is weak.
end: The same whiteboard is now covered in faint, overlapping grey streaks, each a failed attempt that stopped short. The graphite tray below is overflowing with dead markers dropped back in, uncapped and heaped into a mound that spills over its ends. A frozen cascade of markers pours onto the tabletop: one mid-drop, one bouncing, another rolling off the table edge. The acid-lime cap is half buried in the heap. The ivory cloth is smeared grey from wiping. The easel has shifted under the weight of the tray and leans slightly. Dry ink dust hangs in the air, and the spill leads straight back to the tray beneath the streaky board.
apocalypse: A long pale scree slope made of countless dead markers fans down from the foot of an enormous toppled whiteboard, which lies at an angle across the hillside like a collapsed cliff face, its surface cracked and faded with ghostly grey streaks. Its graphite easel legs jut into the sky, bent and rusted. The markers in the scree are sun-bleached and cracked, their graphite barrels dulled by grit. Beyond, a quiet valley fades into haze. At the foot of the slope, a slim graphite refill station rig on four thin legs has lifted one marker from the scree and is filling it through a long nozzle from an acid-lime reservoir tank, a single fresh mark drawn on a flat stone beside it.

title: Empty supply closet
hero: graphite supply shelf with one sticky-note pad
start: A narrow matte graphite supply shelf unit, about the height of a cereal box, stands against a pale neutral wall panel at the back of a tabletop. Its four shelves are bare apart from a single acid-lime sticky-note pad sitting on the middle shelf, its top sheet slightly curled. Faint rectangular dust outlines on the other shelves show where boxes of paper, pens and clips once stood. In the foreground, three small graphite desks sit in an arc facing the closet, each with a neat frosted acrylic pen cup and a thin ivory notepad. Machining lines on the shelf edges and stray fibres on the floor catch the light. The scene is quiet and sparse.
end: The same shelf unit now stands completely bare; the acid-lime sticky-note pad has vanished from it and sits on top of a hoard on the nearest desk. Around the closet, the three desks have become small fortresses: towers of ivory paper reams, frosted pen cups crammed with graphite pens, heaps of binder clips, stacked folders and taped boxes piled high around each chair. A ream is frozen mid-fall from one tower, loose sheets fluttering. A folder has slid off another hoard onto the floor. Dust and paper fibres drift between the piles, and scuff trails on the floor lead from the empty shelves to each desk.
apocalypse: A quiet overgrown plain of pale grass and scattered ivory paper flakes stretches to a soft horizon. In the midground stands the enormous graphite shelf unit, the size of an apartment block, collapsed forward on its knees, shelves bent and streaked with rust and moss. Around it, the old desk hoards have become weathered grassy mounds of fused paper reams, graphite pens and clips half buried in the ground. A cracked frosted pen cup the size of a silo lies on its side. In the foreground, a slim graphite conveyor rig with an acid-lime belt runs from the nearest mound up to the lowest shelf, carrying recovered reams and pens and stacking them neatly back in place.
